newsitem.title: CANADA: Air Canada regional pilots strike hurts net.
newsitem.headline: Air Canada regional pilots strike hurts net.

text.p: A strike by pilots at Air Canada's regional airlines is cutting the company's net profit by about C$7.0-C$8.0 million a month, President and Chief Executive Officer Lamar Durrett said on Friday.
In a telephone conference call, Durrett said he is "cautiously optimistic," however, that the dispute, which began January 10, could be over by the end of this month.

Durrett said he expects Air Canada to report a better operating profit in 1997 after a disappointing 1996 in which operating profit was C$215 million, well below C$275 million in 1995 and the C$300 million forecast last February for 1996.

Unlike his predecessor, Hollis Harris, Durrett declined to make a specific operating or net profit forecast for 1997, but said that as in 1996, revenues in the current fiscal year will continue to be driven mainly by the airline's international routes.

Harris said the airline will continue to expand in 1997, adding about 1,100 employees, most of whom will be flight attendants. The airline plans to add 22 aircraft in 1997, but with the planned retirement of 20 DC-9 jets, the fleet will increase only to 140 aircraft from 138 currently.
Durrett said Air Canada will retain 15 of its DC-9 aircraft, and is in talks on selling some of the DC-9s it will be retiring.

On the operating profit outlook for the year, Durrett said he expects a better performance for several reasons, including expectations that fuel costs, which rose 21 percent in 1996, will stabilize. Also, he sees the airline keeping other costs under control on an employee/passenger mile basis, even though the workforce and fleet will grow.
"On our transborder, we're seeing those routes mature. We're continuing to grow in the international market," he said.
"We actually in the fourth quarter, saw yields firm in the domestic market," Durrett said.
Chief financial officer Robert Peterson said Air Canada will also have a better year in 1997 on the non-operating side because of lower interest payments and less foreign exchange costs.

Peterson the airline took proceeds from the sale in January of the balance of its holding in Continental shares and cash to pay down about C$400 million of debt. Air Canada also has scheduled debt repayments of about C$50-75 million for 1997, he said.

Durrett said he expects a three percent overall reduction in Air Canada's domestic network capacity this year, compared with a planned nine percent reduction at Canadian Airlines. But brisk competition from other airlines, including smaller operators in Western Canadian, will continue in 1997, he said.
"We anticipate that the Canadian domestic market will continue to be an extremely combative are to deal in," Durrett said.
